content.title: About
content.content: Fig, canned – whole or sliced figs preserved in syrup or their own juice. The common fig (Ficus carica) originates from the Mediterranean and Western Asia but is now cultivated in warm regions worldwide. Canning retains the fruit’s sweet, mildly nutty flavor and soft, tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Figs were known in ancient Egypt and used in rituals and medicine.
Dried figs can contain up to 20 % sugar, while canned figs often have about 30 % in the syrup.
The fig is a “false fruit”; the edible part is an enlarged flower receptacle.
In ancient Greece, figs symbolized fertility and abundance.
Canned figs are frequently used in Mediterranean cuisine for desserts, salads, and sauces.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Figs provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in figs protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Figs contain calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, nutrients essential for strong bones.

items.title: Natural source of sugars
items.content: The sugars in figs are natural fruit sugars that provide a quick energy boost.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Canned figs can be sugar‑rich, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Fig allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to figs.

items.title: Preservative content
items.content: Certain cans contain preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate); those sensitive should choose preservative‑free versions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The syrup can be acidic and may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned figs can be eaten straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, salads, cheese plates, or used in baking and sauces. Warm them gently with cinnamon for a simple dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep the jar refrigerated in its original container and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if mold appears or the smell becomes off.
